lastEvent.text: DECISION REQUIRED Herzeg-Bosna · 29 Mar 1993 Vance-Owen: Mostar Records Its Posture PRESIDENTIAL RESPONSE Accept the Vance-Owen ten-province framework HISTORICAL DEFAULT This is the historically attested choice. You are free to choose any option. Acknowledge the VOPP map: three Croat-majority provinces (Mostar, Central Bosnia, Western Herzegovina) are ratified inside the decentralized Bosnia framework. Mate Boban signs for HZ HB at Athens; Zagreb's directive is honored. Herzeg-Bosna morale +4 Herzeg-Bosna Patron Confidence +10 Herzeg-Bosna Int'l Standing +10 Herzeg-Bosna Negotiating Leverage +8 Herzeg-Bosna Internal Cohesion +5 Condition acceptance on provincial-boundary amendments Acknowledge the ten-province framework but condition the signature on amendments to the Central Bosnia and Western Herzegovina provincial boundaries. Zagreb tolerates the conditional posture without full alignment; the central-Bosnia frictions remain unresolved. Herzeg-Bosna morale +2 Herzeg-Bosna Patron Confidence -5 Herzeg-Bosna Negotiating Leverage -5 Herzeg-Bosna Internal Cohesion +3 Condition signature on reciprocal ARBiH acceptance Sign the VOPP framework only if Sarajevo signs simultaneously. A paradoxical joint-front overture: the central-Bosnia friction can be contained if Sarajevo reciprocates, but Zagreb reads the conditional signature as deferring patron direction to a Bosniak counter-signature rather than transmitting it cleanly. Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina / Herzeg-Bosna alliance +0.1 Herzeg-Bosna morale +2 Herzeg-Bosna Patron Confidence -10 Herzeg-Bosna Negotiating Leverage +5 Herzeg-Bosna Internal Cohesion +2 Reject the Vance-Owen ten-province framework Refuse the VOPP map. The HZ HB Presidency defies Zagreb's directive — Tudjman's patron-confidence collapses, the alliance with RBiH breaks further, and international standing falls. The central-Bosnia war continues without a settlement frame; the Croat-majority provinces remain a contested claim rather than a ratified allocation. Through mixed units, municipal committees, and repeated diplomatic briefings, it becomes a working claim: Bosnia is not only a Bosniak war aim, even when Bosniaks carry the heaviest burden. The bargain is difficult and often resented, but it keeps minority cadres in the state project and gives foreign envoys a language they can still defend. Karadzic and Mladic learn the shape of their defense through their lawyers, not through public argument.
